sources.entry: django-rules - A tiny but powerful app for object-level permissions in Django, without a database.

summary.one_liner: django-rules is a small Python library, with an optional Django integration, for defining object-level permissions as rules built from composable predicate functions, with no database queries needed.
summary.what_it_does: It lets you wrap plain callables in a @predicate decorator and combine them with &, |, ^ and ~ into rules, which are stored in a dict-like RuleSet. Rules can be tested directly with test_rule, or registered as Django permissions via add_perm and checked with user.has_perm through the included ObjectPermissionBackend. The README also covers Django integration points: a permission_required view decorator and PermissionRequiredMixin for class-based views, an AutoPermissionRequiredMixin, template tags ({% has_perm %} and {% test_rule %}), and an ObjectPermissionsModelAdmin for per-object checks in the Admin. Predicates can store data in a per-invocation context, bind to self, return None to be skipped, and log evaluations to a 'rules' logger. Predefined predicates include is_authenticated, is_staff, is_superuser, and is_group_member.
use_cases: restricting book edits to the author or editors group
per-object access control in the Django Admin
authorization for Django views and class-based views
building rule-based decision logic without a database
how_to_run: Add 'rules' to INSTALLED_APPS in Django settings
Define predicates with @rules.predicate and register them with rules.add_perm or rules.add_rule
Run tests with ./runtests.sh from a git clone
notable: Predicates work without a database and can be combined with boolean operators
Works as a standalone rule engine outside Django
Per-object permissions for Django views, templates, models Meta options and Admin
Predicates can share per-call context and skip evaluation by returning None
Optional debug logging of each predicate evaluation
caveats: Django integration requires adding a custom authentication backend to settings
Model-based permission declaration (rules_permissions Meta option) works on Python 3 only
Django Admin object permissions need the ObjectPermissionsModelAdmin subclass
